summary: This informational document is a source of information about the Russian federal standard hash function GOST R 34.11-2012, one of the Russian cryptographic standard algorithms. It updates RFC 5831.

eli5.summary: A hash is a fingerprint for data. This describes one country's official way of making fingerprints.

questions: how long is the gost hash code
subtitle: The Russian federal standard hash function that replaced GOST R 34.11-94, with 256-bit and 512-bit outputs.

tldr.problem: Russian cryptographic systems needed a modern standard hash function to replace GOST R 34.11-94, and implementers outside Russia needed an English description of it.
tldr.mechanism: GOST R 34.11-2012 processes a message in 512-bit blocks with an iterated round function built from XOR, a byte substitution, a byte permutation and a linear transformation, then finishes with two extra steps to produce a 512-bit or 256-bit hash code.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is an Informational, independent submission that records the standard and updates RFC 5831. It states that new systems submitted for certification MUST use GOST R 34.11-2012.

today: RFC 6986 is an Informational document that updates RFC 5831, and no RFC obsoletes it or updates it. It describes the standard as published by the Russian Federation in 2012.

sections.title: Scope and Origin of the Standard
sections.content:
RFC 6986 describes the Russian Federal standard hash function GOST R 34.11-2012, one of the Russian cryptographic standard algorithms known as GOST algorithms. The standard defines the algorithm and the calculation procedure for any sequence of binary symbols used in cryptographic methods, including data integrity, authenticity and digital signatures. It is meant to work with the signature algorithm GOST R 34.10-2012.

The standard was developed by the Center for Information Protection and Special Communications of the Federal Security Service of the Russian Federation, with the company InfoTeCS JSC. It was approved by Decree #216 of the Federal Agency on Technical Regulating and Metrology on 07.08.2012. This RFC is an independent submission, not an IETF Standards Track document.
sections.eli5: This is the official rulebook for one way of turning any message into a short fingerprint. Writing it down in an RFC lets people everywhere read the same rules.

sections.title: Replacing GOST R 34.11-94
sections.content:
GOST R 34.11-2012 is intended to replace the older national standard GOST R 34.11-94, which is the function described in RFC 5831. This document updates RFC 5831.

The text sets out a transition rule. From 1st January 2013, GOST R 34.11-94 is superseded. All new systems presented for certification MUST use GOST R 34.11-2012 and MAY also use GOST R 34.11-94 to stay compatible with existing systems. Use of GOST R 34.11-94 in current systems is allowed for at least a 5-year period.
sections.eli5: It is like a school switching to a new official pencil. New classes must use the new one, and old classes may keep using the old one for a while.

sections.title: Hash Lengths and Fixed Parameters
sections.content:
The standard defines two hash functions with different output sizes: a hash code of 512 bits and a hash code of 256 bits. They share the same internal machinery. The input message M may be any bit string shorter than 2^512 bits.

They differ in the initializing value IV. For the 512-bit function IV is all zeros (0^512). For the 256-bit function IV is the byte 00000001 repeated 64 times.

The RFC also fixes the constants the algorithm needs. These are a nonlinear substitution Pi on 8-bit values, a byte permutation Tau over 64 positions, a 64 by 64 binary matrix A that defines a linear transformation, and iteration constants C[1] to C[12], each given in hexadecimal.
sections.eli5: There are two sizes of fingerprint, a big one and a small one. Both use the same lookup tables and secret-looking numbers that everyone agrees on in advance.

sections.title: Transformations and the Round Function
sections.content:
Four building blocks work on 512-bit values. X[k] XORs the value with a key k. S replaces each of the 64 bytes using the substitution Pi. P reorders the bytes using the permutation Tau. L splits the value into eight 64-bit pieces and applies the matrix transformation to each.

The round function is g_N(h, m) = E(LPS(h xor N), m) xor h xor m. It mixes a 512-bit chaining value h with a 512-bit message block m and a counter N. The inner function E is a block-cipher-like routine that runs 13 round keys K[1] to K[13] through alternating key XORs and LPS steps. The keys are derived from each other: K[1] is the starting key, and each later K[i] is LPS(K[i-1] xor C[i-1]).
sections.eli5: Imagine a blender with four buttons: swap letters, shuffle positions, stir in bits, and add a secret number. The round function presses those buttons many times so the input is thoroughly mixed up.

sections.title: Calculating the Hash Code
sections.content:
The procedure starts with h set to IV, and a length counter N and a checksum EPSILON both set to zero. While at least 512 bits of the message remain, it takes the last 512-bit block m, sets h := g_N(h, m), adds 512 to N and adds m to EPSILON. It then repeats on what is left.

When fewer than 512 bits remain, the final piece is padded: zero bits, then a single 1 bit, then the remaining message, to fill a block. The round function is applied once more and N and EPSILON are updated. Two finishing steps follow: h := g_0(h, N) and then h := g_0(h, EPSILON). For the 256-bit function, only the 256 most significant bits of that last result are kept. The final h is the hash code H(M).

Section 10 of the RFC gives two worked examples, each for both the 512-bit and the 256-bit function. They are informative and not a normative part of the standard.
sections.eli5: The hash reads the message in big chunks, stirring each chunk into a running mixture. At the end it stirs in the total length and a running sum, then hands back the mixture as the fingerprint.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC's Security Considerations section is a single sentence: this entire document is about security considerations. It adds no further analysis.

The document does define what it means by a collision-resistant hash function. It must be computationally infeasible to find an input for a given output, to find a second input matching a given input's output, or to find any two distinct inputs with the same output.
sections.eli5: A good fingerprint maker should make it practically impossible to fake a message that matches someone else's fingerprint.
